title: Helping Others Combine and Apply Their Strengths
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case that knowing your strengths isn't the same as knowing how to combine them for maximum effect, and that this combinatory insight is a place where leaders add real value as coaches. Using a hypothetical team member who is both witty and empathetic, the piece illustrates how pairing two individually familiar strengths can create an emergent new capability — like diffusing tense situations — that the person wouldn't have discovered alone. The author frames this as a distinct coaching skill separate from simple strengths-identification.
points: Most people already know their individual strengths through a lifetime of feedback, but rarely know how to combine them for amplified effect.
Leaders add unique value by pointing out non-obvious combinations of strengths (e.g., humor plus empathy) tied to a specific outcome or situation.
Naming a strength combination and attaching it to a concrete goal is what makes the insight actionable rather than abstract.
Once shown how to combine strengths, team members typically begin experimenting on their own and are often surprised by the results.
quotes: Knowing yourself, especially your strengths and weaknesses, is essential work for personal development and for reaching your potential.
What is not as obvious to others is that when strengths are combined in specific situations, they often amplify each other, creating a brand-new strength.

An exceptional leader might point out to this team member how their humor and empathy together might be an even more powerful combination that could work to diffuse tense and high-pressure situations.
Learning how and when to combine key strengths doesn’t come naturally to anyone.
A good head and a good heart are always a formidable combination.
